items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Joe had been in France and other parts of Europe before the last war, and we had met in Boudon's many times.

ctx.x: In December 1940, Barney Josephson branched out and opened a Cafe Society Uptown on East 58th Street, and it was a real plushy joint. The Cafe Society Downtown was not a very large place, and there was only one small dressing room for musicians and entertainers. But at the Uptown, the whole building was occupied by the club and there was a big dressing room for the two bands, the Golden Gate Quartet and the Boogie Woogies. There were at least 4 other dressing rooms quite large and they were all on the third floor.

The club featured Teddy Wilson and Eddie South's orchestra, the Gates, the Boogies without Joe Turner, Hazel Scott and a comedian named Penner. Eddie South was a violinist known as "the Dark Angel" of that instrument and had been trained by some of the finest violin professors in Europe and especially in Hungaria. He was a classical musician that could play jazz also and had recorded some duets with the famous Stephane Grappelly in France.

Eddie had the bassist Dole Dickens, a fine classical and jazz pianist named Stanley Facey and the well known drummer Gordon "Specs" Powell to accompany him. Eddie was one of the attractions in the floor show and also played for dancing when we had our intermissions.

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I know that three of them were discovered by and sponsored by John Hammond... there was a great blues singer named 'Big' Joe Turner whom the two boogie woogie pianists accompanied.

ctx.x: This club, which was actually called Cafe Society Downtown, was at Sheridan Square and was owned by a man named Barney Josephson. The manager was Harold Johnson and a great barman called Lew. I will mention why Lew was a great barman to me later. There were four acts in the show and I know that three of them were discovered by and sponsored by John Hammond.

Boogie Woogie was popular and John had put it together the three greatest exponents of that style of piano playing. They were Meade Lux Lewis, Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons. But the Cafe only Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons were working as a team, and there was a great blues singer named "Big" Joe Turner whom the two boogie woogie pianists accompanied. And the three of them would really rock the joint every night. And they could drink plenty of booze and carry it well.

Another act was called the Golden Gate Quartet. Their names were Bill Johnson, Clyde Redick, Wilson and . They had a style of singing gospel songs which I had never heard before. In fact I didn't know anything about gospel singing except what I had heard in Baptist churches. But this was more like Holy-Holy singing to me, because it had a jazz rhythm and these fellows slap their thighs with their hands in four-four rhythm; and Yank accompanied them on drums with wire brushes on the snare drum and the joint kept…
